rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reciting the verse at bedtime is said to protect a house from theft; a thief repeatedly gathered a migrant's belongings but could not open the door, and the owner said his house was protected.
rows.anchor: هو أمان من السرق وأن رجلا من المهاجرين تلاها حين أخذ مضجعه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In Mecca, while the Prophet was concealed, he recited aloud in prayer; polytheists cursed the Qur'an, its sender, and its bearer, so God instructed him to moderate his voice while remaining audible to companions.
rows.anchor: أخرج أحمد والبخاري ومسلم والترمذي والنسائي وابن حبان وغيرهم عن ابن عباس قال : نزلت ورسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here prayer can stand metonymically for its recitation, one of its parts, or the phrase can mean the recitation of your prayer; recitation includes the basmala and other verses.
rows.anchor: وظاهره أن المراد بالصلاة القراءة التي هي أحد أجزائها مجازا ويجوز أن يكون الكلام على تقدير مضاف

rows.speaker: سعيد
rows.claim: A report specifies the basmala: the Prophet raised his voice with it, and polytheists associated al-Rahman with Musaylima, then mocked with clapping and whistling; this reading especially fits the preceding verse.
rows.anchor:
أخرج ابن أبي شيبة في المصنف عن سعيد
قال : كان النبي

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Abu Bakr prayed at night very quietly and Umar very loudly; after they reported their disagreement, the Prophet told Abu Bakr to raise his voice somewhat and Umar to lower his.
rows.anchor: ابن أبي حاتم عن الربيع قال : كان أبو بكر إذا صلى من الليل خفض صوته جدا وكان عمر

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Asked why he prayed quietly, Abu Bakr said he was confiding in his Lord, who already knew his need.
rows.anchor: قيل لأبي بكر : لم تصنع هذا فقال : أناجي ربي وقد عرف حاجتي

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Asked why he prayed loudly, Umar said the sound drove Satan away and awakened a sleepy person.
rows.anchor: وقيل لعمر : لم تصنع هذا قال : اطرد الشيطان وأوقظ الوسنان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another explanation says not to make every prayer loud or every prayer quiet, but to recite aloud in some prayers such as Maghrib and Isha and quietly in others.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أن المعنى لا تجهر بصلاتك كلها ولا تخافت بها كلها وابتغ بين ذلك سبيلا

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections interprets prayer here as supplication; Mujahid and Ibn Abbas are also reported to hold this, with people loudly saying prayers such as “Have mercy on me.”
rows.anchor: أخرج الشيخان وغيرهما عن عائشة قالت : إنما نزلت هذه الآية

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن شداد
rows.claim: Bedouins from Banu Tamim loudly asked the Prophet for camels and children after his salutation, and the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن شداد أن أعرابا من بني تميم كانوا إذا سلم النبي

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A second report interprets prayer as the tashahhud; Arabs reportedly recited their tashahhud loudly, prompting revelation.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية أخرى عن عائشة أن الصلاة هنا التشهد وكان الأعراب كما نقل عن ابن سيرين يجهرون بتشهدهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: A literal interpretation of ritual prayer says do not pray for show or abandon prayer out of embarrassment; a similar interpretation is transmitted from Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: فقد أخرج ابن عساكر عن الحسن أنه قال : المعنى لا تصل الصلاة رياء ولا تدعها حياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators prefer Ibn Abbas's first explanation: the command concerns the volume of Qur'anic recitation in prayer.
rows.anchor: والأكثرون على التفسير المروي عنه أولا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Whispering means speech so quiet that the speaker cannot hear it; Ibn Masud says that anyone who makes his own ears hear has not whispered.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا قال ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling moderation a path evokes a way toward which people direct themselves and by which capable travelers reach their goal; Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir and Abu Qilaba transmit that the best affairs are middle ones.
rows.anchor: والتعبير عن الأمر الوسط بالسبيل باعتبار أنه أمر يتوجه إليه المتوجهون ويؤمه المقتدرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators consider the verse still operative; one view calls it abrogated based on an Ibn Abbas report that the Meccan moderation rule lapsed after the Hijra.
rows.anchor: والآية على ما يقتضيه كلام الأكثرين محكمة وقيل منسوخة بناء على ما أخرجه ابن مردويه وابن أبي حاتم عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposed abrogation by the command to call upon God humbly and privately is dismissed as untenable.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي منسوخة بقوله تعالى ( ادعوا ربكم تضرعا وخفية ) وهو كما ترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rulings on reciting louder than needed and whispering in the defined sense are treated in fiqh works, to which readers are referred.
rows.anchor: حكم رفع الصوت بالقراءة فوق الحاجة وحكم المخافتة بالمعنى الذي سمعته المسطوران في كتب الفقه

rows.speaker: أبو رزين
rows.claim: Abu Razin transmits a codex reading attributed to Abd Allah: “Do not whisper your voice nor raise it.”
rows.anchor: ابن أبي داود في المصاحف عن أبي رزين قال قرأ عبد الله ( ولا تخافت بصوتك ولا تعال به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial that God took a child refutes Jews, Christians, Banu Mulayh, and claims that Uzayr, the Messiah, or angels are God's children; denying adoption entails denying biological offspring, explicitly denied elsewhere.
rows.anchor: رد على اليهود والنصارى وبني مليح حيث قالوا : عزير ابن الله والمسيح ابن الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No partner in dominion” may refute dualists who posit partners in lordship, or figuratively deny partners in divinity and thus refute idolaters.
rows.anchor: ظاهره انه رد على الثنوية وهم المشركون في الربوبية ويجوز أن يكون كناية عن نفي الشركة في الألوهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No ally from humiliation” can mean God needs no protector, with min attached to ally and implying protection, or that He allies with no one because of lowliness, with min causal and wilaya retaining love; neither reading implies divine need.
rows.anchor: أي ناصر ومانع له سبحانه من الذل لاعتزازه تعالى بنفسه فمن صلة لولي وضمن معنى المنع والنصر

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf's preferred reading treats any divine alliance or aid as pure grace, not need; aid perfects the one aided, and the author considers this a good interpretation.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب صاحب الكشف وهو حسن

rows.speaker: الفاضل الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi assigns the two interpretations of “ally from humiliation” to a figure of speech that avoids implying either divine need or ordinary reciprocity.
rows.anchor: وجعل ذلك على الوجهين الفاضل الطيبي من ذاك الأسلوب

rows.speaker: الحواشي الشهابية
rows.claim: A gloss explains the second reading as denying that God has a master to whom He resorts; a believer's “ally” instead means one who graciously manages the believer's affairs, a different sense of wilaya.
rows.anchor: في بيان ثاني الوجهين أن المراد نفي أن يكون له تعالى مولى يلتجيء هو سبحانه إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An interpretation making min partitive and supplying “people of humiliation,” meaning Jews and Christians, is deemed unworthy of consideration.
rows.anchor: ومن عجيب ما قيل إن ( من الذل ) في موضع الصفة لولي ومن فيه للتبعيض

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Although praise usually concerns voluntary acts, these negative attributes merit praise because they establish God's necessary existence and self-sufficiency, while all else depends on Him as generous giver.
rows.anchor: يدفع بأنه لاق وصفه تعالى بما ذكر بكلمة التحميد لأنه يدل على نفي الامكان المقتضي للإحتياج

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Denial of child, partner, and need for a defender also implies their positive opposites: generosity, unrestricted action, and self-sufficiency; the author says literal praise for these attributes is also coherent.
rows.anchor: لك أن تتخذ نفي هذه الصفات وهي ذرائع منع المعروف أما الولد فلأنه مبخلة وأما الشريك فلأنه مانع من التصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says “praise belongs to God” already implies divinity deserves praise, but that argument needs reconsideration if one rejects derivation of the proper name Allah.
rows.anchor: بأن ما ذكره من أن في الحمد لله ما ينبيء أن الإلهية تقتضي الحمد لا يتم على مذهب ما نعي الإشتقاق

rows.speaker: العلامة الطيبي
rows.claim: The verse exhaustively denies every possible barrier to giving blessings: a superior, inferior, or equal; it moves upward through these ranks and denies all, establishing God's perfection and entitlement to magnification.
rows.anchor: الآية على ما قال العلامة الطيبي من التقسيم الحاصر لأن المانع من إيتاء النعم إما فوقه سبحانه وتعالى أو دونه أو مثله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takbir is Arabic's strongest expression for glorification and reverence; its command, reinforced by an indefinite verbal noun, signals that human speech and effort cannot encompass God's greatness.
rows.anchor: والتكبير أبلغ لفظة للعرب في معنى التعظيم والاجلال وفي الأمر بذلك بعد ما تقدم مؤكدا بالمصدر المنكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After striving in praise and worship, the servant can only stand humbly in the lowliness of incapacity and confess inability to fulfill God's due.
rows.anchor: فلم يبق إلا الوقوف بأقدام المذلة في حضيض القصور والإعتراف بالعجز عن القيام بحقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several transmitters say the Prophet taught a young boy from Banu Abd al-Muttalib to recite the verse seven times once he could speak.
rows.anchor: وروى غير واحد أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يعلم الغلام من بني عبد المطلب إذا أفصح الحمد لله إلى آخر الآية سبع مرات

rows.speaker: معاذ
rows.claim: A report from Muadh says the Prophet named this passage the Verse of Might.
rows.anchor: كما أخرج أحمد والطبراني عن معاذ آية العز

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet taught a ragged, ill and distressed man a trust-and-praise formula ending with this verse; later the man looked well, saying he had kept repeating it.
rows.anchor: أبو يعلى وابن السني عن أبي هريرة قال : خرجت أنا ورسول الله

rows.speaker: إسماعيل بن أبي فديك
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Fudayk reports from the Prophet that whenever an affair distressed him, Gabriel appeared and told him to say a formula including trust in the Ever-Living and this verse.
rows.anchor: عن إسماعيل بن أبي فديك قال : قال رسول الله

rows.speaker: فاطمة بنت رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet taught Fatimah a bedtime litany ending with the whole verse; whoever recites it before sleep is protected from devils and vermin that night.
rows.anchor: قال لها إذا أخذت مضجعك فقولي : الحمد لله الكافي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author notes a subtle connection between this surah's opening and the preceding surah's closing.
rows.anchor: هذا وما ألطف المناسبة بين ابتداء هذه السورة وهذا الختام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning that opponents nearly tempted the Prophet cautions him against violating the conditions of divine love and hints at his reaching the station of spiritual firmness.
rows.anchor: وأن كادوا ليفتنونك إلى آخره تنبيه لحبيبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mystical account distinguishes five prayers: communion at the hidden station, vision at the spirit, private converse at the secret, presence at the heart, and obedience at the soul.
rows.anchor: وذكر أن الصلاة على خمسة أقسام صلاة المواصلة والمناغاة في مقام الخفي وصلاة المشاهدة في مقام الروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this symbolism, the sun's decline marks unity's withdrawal from the servant's existence through annihilation; no prayer occurs at the zenith because the servant has no existence or self-awareness then.
rows.anchor: فدلوك الشمس إشارة إلى زوال شمس الوحدة عن الاستواء على وجود العبد بالفناء المحض فإنه لا صلاة في حال الاستواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer becomes due as the servant's shadow of existence appears, either while veiled from creation before union or while abiding after union.
rows.anchor: وإنما تجب بالزوال وحدوث ظل وجود العبد سواء عند الاحتجاب بالخلق وهو حالة الفرق قبل الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nightfall symbolizes the darkening night of the lower self, while dawn recitation symbolizes the heart's dawn; dawn's Qur'an is witnessed by angels of night and day and signifies the heart's lights replacing traits of the self.
rows.anchor: وغسق الليل إشارة إلى غسق ليل النفس وقرآن الفجر إشارة إلى قرآن فجر القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mystical ranking calls union the most subtle prayer, witnessing (asr) the best, secret prayer (maghrib) the lightest, the soul's prayer (isha) most stabilizing, and presence (fajr) most effective against Satan.
rows.anchor: وأدل الصلوات وألطفها صلاة المواصلة وأفضلها صلاة الشهود المشار إليها بصلاة العصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night vigil is an added act of obedience specific to the Prophet either because the soul's station especially needs extra prayer, or because night is the lover's solitude with the Beloved, Muhammad being the greatest beloved.
rows.anchor: قيل لكونه علامة مقام النفس فيجب تخصيصه بزيادة الطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The praised station is the joining of the deficient to the complete and the complete to the more perfect.
rows.anchor: وهو مقام الحاق الناقص بالكامل والكامل بالأكمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mystical reading makes entry into a true entrance arrival at unity within gathered oneness, without turning toward another; true departure returns to multiplicity with God-given existence, free from change or deviation.
rows.anchor: حضرة الوحدة في عين الجمع ( مدخل صدق ) إدخالا مرضيا بلا آفة زيغ البصر إلى الإلتفات إلى الغير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requested supporting authority is an argument that brings steadfastness and spiritual firmness.
rows.anchor: واجعل لي من لدنك سلطانا نصيرا ) حجة ناصرة بالتثبيت والتمكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the mystical interpretation, the coming of truth is the appearance of necessary existence, while falsehood's vanishing is the disappearance of contingent existence.
rows.anchor: جاء الحق ) أي ظهر الوجود الثابت وهو الوجود الواجبي ( وزهق الباطل ) وهو الوجود الامكاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sound hadith calls Labid's verse “Indeed, everything apart from God is false” the truest statement spoken by a poet.
rows.anchor:
ففي الحديث الصحيح أصدق كلمة
قالها شاعر كلمة لبيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who know the Qur'an's realities prostrate when it is recited and weep from its majesty or from longing for its source and love of meeting it.
rows.anchor: فيه من الأسرار ( ويخرون للأذقان يبكون ) لعظمته أو شوقا لمنزله

rows.speaker: أبو يعقوب السوسي
rows.claim: Al-Susi distinguishes weeping from God (fear of what destiny decreed), on God (regret at losing Him), for God (at His mention and promise or threat), and by God (seeing Him as cause of one's tears).
rows.anchor: قال أبو يعقوب السوسي : البكاء على أنواع بكاء من الله تعالى وهو أن يبكي خوفا مما جرى به القلم

rows.speaker: القاسم
rows.claim: Al-Qasim classifies tears as ignorance over what is unknown, scholars' regret over shortcomings, the righteous' fear of loss, imams' fear of being driven onward, and spiritual knights' awe; he says monotheists do not weep.
rows.anchor: وقال القاسم : البكاء على وجوه بكاء الجهال على ما جهلوا وبكاء العلماء على ما قصروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse gestures toward devotional audition, and listening to the Qur'an is the noblest such audition, bringing spirit and delight.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية إشارة ما إلى السماع ولا أشرف من سماع القرآن فهو الروح والريحان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Esoterically, calling on Allah signifies annihilation in the divine essence, while calling on al-Rahman signifies annihilation in the attribute of mercy, the mother of attributes and the means by which God shows mercy to creatures.
rows.anchor: قيل دعاء الله بالفناء في الذات ودعاء الرحمن بالفناء في الصفة وصفة الرحمانية هي أم الصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whichever of these two stations is sought, the beautiful names belong to God rather than the annihilated servant: the servant is absent in essence-annihilation, and the name al-Rahman is unique to God in attribute-annihilation.
rows.anchor: أيا ما طلبت من هذين المقامين ( فله ) تعالى في هذين المقامين ( الأسماء الحسنى ) لا لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Futuhat, divine names belong both to Allah and al-Rahman, but Allah is invoked by a name's meaning and al-Rahman by its form; both forms ultimately signify the same meaning.
rows.anchor: وفي الفتوحات المكية أنه تعالى جعل الأسماء الحسنى لله كما هي للرحمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Breath of the Merciful manifests divine words in the void where the world appears; humans invoke God through the forms of names made from their breath and letter-combinations, serving as translators of the divine names.
rows.anchor: لأن الرحمن هو المنعوت بالنفس وبالنفس ظهرت الكلمات

rows.speaker: ابن عربي
rows.claim: The forms arising from the Merciful's breath have meanings behind them, like spirits behind letters; these meanings are divine-name realities beyond qualification and are related to the humanly uttered forms as meanings to letters.
rows.anchor: وخلف تلك الصور المعاني التي هي كالأرواح للأسماء الإلهية التي يذكر الحق بها نفسه

rows.speaker: ابن عربي
rows.claim: The two permitted invocations are either the forms of merciful breath present in cosmic aspirations within our spirits, or the names articulated by our own breath as translation; one may attend to the meaning of Allah or the form of al-Rahman.
rows.anchor: فإن شئنا دعوناه بصور الأسماء النفسية الرحمانية وهي الهمم الكونية التي في أرواحنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says this difficult account does not make the verse's invocation a simple supplication in the earlier sense.
rows.anchor: وهو كلام يعسر فهمه إلا على من شاء الله تعالى بيد أنه ليس فيه حمل الدعاء على ما سمعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has no child by generation and no other true owner shares dominion; causes are merely instruments, and all things are truly God's work, as with a bed attributed to its carpenter although the carpenter is also an instrument.
rows.anchor: فلا مدخل لغيره تعالى في ملكية شيء على الحقيقة وما يوجد بسبب ليس السبب إلا آلة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers readers to Ibn Arabi's discussion in chapter 198 for the account of ownership and notes that his prior explanation already covers the phrase about an ally from humiliation.
rows.anchor: وللشيخ قدس سره كلام في هذا المقام يفصح عن بعض هذا ذكره في الباب الثامن والتسعين بعد المائة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One interpretation says magnifying God means recognizing that one cannot magnify Him except through Him.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم تكبيره تعالى أن تعلم أنك لا تطيق أن تكبره إلا به

rows.speaker: ابن عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn Ata says magnification is honoring God's gifts and beneficence in the heart while recognizing one's failure to give thanks, since His blessings cannot be counted or exhausted.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطاء تكبيره عز وجل بتعظيم منته وإحسانه في القلب بالعلم بالتقصير في الشكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is also called “The Companions of the Cave,” according to a report collected by Ibn Mardawayh; an Ibn Abbas report says the Torah calls it “the barrier,” protecting its reciter from fire, but al-Bayhaqi grades that report munkar.
rows.anchor: ويقال سورة أصحاب الكهف كما في حديث أخرجه ابن مردويه وروى البيهقي من حديث ابن عباس مرفوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority say the whole surah is Meccan, a view chosen by al-Dani and transmitted from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr; a report from Anas says it descended all at once with seventy thousand angels.
rows.anchor: وهي مكية كلها في المشهور واختاره الداني وروي عن ابن عباس وابن الزبير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report, also attributed to Qatada, says the surah is Meccan except “Restrain yourself” (18:28).
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنها مكية إلا قوله تعالى ( واصبر نفسك ) الآية فمدني وروي ذلك عن قتادة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the surah is Meccan except its opening through “barren ground” (18:8) and the passage beginning “Indeed, those who believe” through the end.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل : هي مكية إلا أولها إلى ( جرزا ) وقوله تعالى : ( إن الذين آمنوا ) إلى آخرها فمدني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Regional verse counts differ: Basrans count 111, Kufans 110, Syrians 106, and Hijazis 105.
rows.anchor: وهي مائة وإحدى عشرة آية عند البصريين ومائة وعشرة عند الكوفيين ومائة وست عند الشاميين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One coherence argument is that the preceding surah opens with glorification and this one with praise, paired on the scales and repeatedly joined in expressions such as “glorify with praise”; their endings and beginnings also correspond.
rows.anchor: افتتاح تلك بالتسبيح وهذه بالتحميد وهما مقترنان في الميزان وسائر الكلام نحو ( فسبح بحمد ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further comparison distinguishes the preceding surah's final praise as essential praise and this surah's opening praise as indicating deservedness other than by essence.
rows.anchor: فرق بينهما بأن الحمد الأول ظاهر الحمد الذاتي والحمد المفتتح به في هذه يدل على الإستحقاق الغير الذاتي

rows.speaker: جلال السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti says Jews prompted the polytheists to ask about the spirit, the Cave companions, and Dhu al-Qarnayn; the spirit's answer ends the previous surah and the other two answers occur here, while the spirit was separated because its reality was not explained.
rows.anchor: عن ثلاثة أشياء عن الروح وعن قصة أصحاب الكهف وعن قصة ذي القرنين

rows.speaker: جلال السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti offers another link: both the Night Journey and spirit exceed ordinary rational comprehension, or the Journey ascends from the higher realm while the spirit descends from it; he quotes Ibn Sina's poem about the spirit's descent.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنما ذكر هناك لما أن الإسراء متضمن العروج إلى المحل الأرفع والروح متصفة بالهبوط من ذلك المحل

rows.speaker: جلال السيوطي
rows.claim: Because Jews heard that human knowledge is little, this surah's story of Moses and Khidr demonstrates God's immeasurable knowledge and supports the preceding judgment; a report says the Jews claimed the Torah contained all knowledge before the sea-as-ink verse answered them.
rows.anchor: استظهر على ذلك بقصة موسى نبي بني إسرائيل مع الخضر عليهما السلام التي كان سبب ذكر العلم والأعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous surah's statement that God would gather the people is expanded here through the account of the barrier's leveling and the gathering and display of Hell.
rows.anchor: لما قال سبحانه هناك ( فإذا جاء وعد الآخرة جئنا بكم لفيفا ) شرح ذلك هنا وبسطه بقوله سبحانه ( فإذا جاء وعد ربي جعله دكاء

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Umar says that reciting the Cave on Friday brings light from beneath one's feet to the sky until the Resurrection and forgives the sins between Fridays.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن مردويه عن ابن عمر مرفوعا

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Several transmitters report from Abu Said al-Khudri that Friday recitation of the Cave lights the distance between its reader and the Sacred House.
rows.anchor: وروى غير واحد عن أبي سعيد الخدري من قرأ سورة الكهف في يوم الجمعة أضاء له من النور

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: Umm Musa reports that al-Hasan ibn Ali used to recite the surah every night.
rows.anchor: كما أخرج أبو عبيد والبيهقي عن أم موسى يقرأها كل ليلة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مغفل
rows.claim: A report from Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal says Satan does not enter that night a house where the Cave is recited.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن مردويه عن عبد الله بن مغفل مرفوعا البيت الذي تقرأ فيه سورة الكهف لا يدخله الشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several imams recommend reciting the surah on Friday and its eve, and repeating the recitation.
rows.anchor: وإلى سنية قراءتها يوم الجمعة وكذا ليلتها ذهب غير واحد من الأئمة وقالوا بندب تكرار قراءتها

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: A report from Abu al-Darda says memorizing the first ten verses protects against the Dajjal's trial; another version says to recite the final ten.
rows.anchor: من حفظ عشر آيات من أول سورة الكهف عصم من فتنة الدجال

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: A further report, authenticated by al-Tirmidhi, says reciting three verses from the beginning of the Cave protects from the Dajjal's trial.
rows.anchor: وأخرج الترمذي وصححه عنه مرفوعا من قرأ ثلاث آيات من أول الكهف عصم

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report attributed to Aisha says whoever recites the final five verses before sleep is raised by God at whichever hour of the night He wills; the author says he tried it repeatedly.
rows.anchor: مرفوعا إن من قرأ الخمس الأواخر منها عند نومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “Book” is the complete Qur'an, self-sufficient in perfection and uniquely deserving the name, or the revelation already sent at that point; the relative clause explains why God deserves praise and magnifies the revelation.
rows.anchor: الكتاب ( الكامل الغني عن الوصف بالكمال المعروف بذلك من بين سائر الكتب الحقيق باختصاص اسم الكتاب به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Muhammad God's servant honors both messenger and revelation and indicates that a messenger must be the sender's servant, unlike Christian claims about Jesus.
rows.anchor: بالعبد مضافا إلى ضميره تعالى من الإشارة إلى تعظيمه عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The direct object “Book” is delayed after the prepositional phrase so that “and He made no crookedness in it” can immediately follow it.
rows.anchor: وتأخير المفعول الصريح عن الجار والمجرور مع أن حقه التقديم عليه ليتصل به قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denied crookedness includes defects of grammatical wording or eloquence, contradiction in meaning, falsehood, or calling to other than God.
rows.anchor: أي شيئا من العوج باختلال اللفظ من جهة الإعراب ومخالفة الفصاحة وتناقض المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A lexical distinction assigns kasra in ʿiwaj to inward or intelligible deviation and fatha in ʿawaj to physical deviation visible to the eye.
rows.anchor: هو بكسر العين ما يدرك بفتح العين وبفتح العين ما يدرك بفتح العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distinction is challenged because the earth in 20:107 is physical; one answer says the verse denies subtle unevenness detectable only by geometry and insight, though “you do not see” seems to describe sight; Ibn al-Sikkit says the kasra form is broader.
rows.anchor: وأورد عليه قوله تعالى في شأن الأرض ( لا ترى فيها عوجا ولا أمتا ) فإن الأرض محسوسة واعوجاجها

rows.speaker: المرزوقي
rows.claim: Al-Marzuki, in his commentary on al-Fasih, chooses that the kasra and fatha forms of ʿiwaj/ʿawaj have no difference in meaning.
rows.anchor: واختار المرزوقي في شرح الفصيح أنه لا فرق بينهما

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Qiyaman is glossed as “upright” by al-Dahhak, with the same explanation also transmitted from Ibn Abbas: the Book has no flaw in wording or meaning.
rows.anchor: أي مستقيما كما أخرجه ابن المنذر عن الضحاك وروي أيضا عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an is balanced: its duties impose neither excessive hardship nor neglect needed guidance; as the final scripture revealed to the final Messenger, it leaves no needed matter unattended.
rows.anchor: إنه معتدل لا إفراط فيما اشتمل عليه من التكاليف حتى يشق على العباد ولا تفريط فيه بإهمال ما يحتاج إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view treats qiyaman as repeating the preceding description for emphasis.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد منه ما أريد مما قبله وذكره للتأكيد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the Qur'an is a guardian over other revealed books and testifies to their truth, making qiyaman a new assertion rather than mere repetition.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء : المراد قيما على سائر الكتب السماوية شاهدا بصحتها

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim says the Qur'an stands for people's welfare, covering worldly and afterlife needs because it orders their lives; this too makes qiyaman a new assertion, and it is complete in itself and completes others.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم : المراد قيما بمصالح العباد متكفلا بها وببيانها لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under the new-assertion readings, the Qur'an is either true and confirming of other books or free of defects and full of virtues.
rows.anchor: فكأنه قيل كتابا صادقا في نفسه مصدقا لغيره أو كتابا خاليا عن النقائص حاليا بالفضائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qiyaman may be accusative after an implied “made it upright,” as an independent sentence or coordinated clause, though deleting the conjunction before the coordinated clause is awkward.
rows.anchor: ونصبه بمضمر أي جعله قيما على أن الجملة مستأنفة أو جعله قيما على أنها معطوفة

rows.speaker: حفص
rows.claim: Hafs pauses briefly after ʿiwaja, then resumes with qiyaman.
rows.anchor: وكان حفص يسكت على ( عوجا ) سكتة خفيفة ثم يقول : ( قيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several scholars prefer parsing qiyaman as a circumstantial accusative attached to “for it”: God made the Book without crookedness while it is upright and free from flaw or excess.
rows.anchor: واختار غير واحد أنه على الحال من الضمير في ( له ) أي لم يجعل له عوجا حال كونه مستقيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some find that circumstantial parsing awkward if “upright” simply means “without crookedness.”
rows.anchor: نعم قيل : إن جعله حالا من الضمير مع تفسير المستقيم بالخالي عن العوج ركيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent awkwardness can be avoided by taking qiyaman as an emphatic circumstantial state, as in “then you turned away, retreating.”
rows.anchor: وتعقبه بعضهم بأنه تندفع الركاكة بالحمل على الحالة المؤكدة كما في قوله تعالى ( ثم وليتم مدبرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parsing qiyaman as a state of the Book is challenged because it would coordinate before the relative clause is complete; one answer makes “and He made no crookedness” an explanatory completion of “the Book,” as with the disputed analysis of 2:217.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون حالا من الكتاب واعترض بأنه يلزم حينئذ العطف قبل تمام الصلة

rows.speaker: الأصبهاني
rows.claim: Al-Asfahani prefers treating the “and He made no crookedness” clause as a circumstantial clause of the Book, alongside qiyaman.
rows.anchor: وأيضا يجوز أن يكون الواو في ( ولم يجعل ) للحال والجملة بعده حال من ( الكتاب ) كقيما واختاره الأصبهاني

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan objects that the circumstantial parsing requires two uncoordinated states from one subject, which many of his colleagues disallow; an argument from al-Farisi's rule about mixed nominal and clausal predicates is answered as contrary to most grammarians and inapplicable by analogy.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان : إن ذاك على مذهب من يجوز وقوع حالين من ذي حال واحد بغير عطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The actual order is defensible because qiyaman describes stable intrinsic uprightness, which might still conceal a slight bend; negating any bend first closes that possibility and receives emphasis.
rows.anchor: ولما كان ( قيما ) يفيد استقامة ذاتية أو ثابتة لكونه صفة مشبهة وصيغة مبالغة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says pairing uprightness with the denial of crookedness adds emphasis, because something apparently upright may hide a slight defect on close inspection.
rows.anchor: فرب مستقيم مشهود له بالاستقامة ولا يخلو من أدنى عوج عند السبر والتصفح

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Razi argues that “no crookedness” means the Qur'an is perfect in itself and qiyaman means it perfects others, so the given order is logically necessary; the author objects if he knew the inversion was reported from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.
rows.anchor: قول الإمام إن قوله تعالى : ( لم يجعل له عوجا ) يدل على كونه مكملا في ذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the pronoun in “for it” refers to God's servant rather than the Book, the earlier syntactic analyses no longer apply.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن ضمير ( له ) عائد على ( عبده ) وحينئذ لا يتأتى جميع التخاريج الإعرابية السابقة

rows.speaker: أبان بن ثعلب
rows.claim: Aban ibn Taghlib is reported to read qiyaman with a kasra on qaf and a light, open ya.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبان بن ثعلب ( قيما ) بكسر القاف وفتح الباء المخففة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading in some Companion codices adds “rather, He made it upright”; the author classifies this as explanatory gloss, not a Qur'anic reading.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض مصاحف الصحابة ( ولم يجعل له عوجا لكنه قيما ) وحمل ذلك على أنه تفسير لا قراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose-lam in “to warn” links to “sent down,” supporting the Salaf and Maturidi view that God's acts have purposes; those who deny that read it as a result-lam.
rows.anchor: لينذر ( متعلق بأنزل واللام للتعليل واستدل به من قال بتعليل أفعال الله تعالى بالأغراض كالسلف والماتريدية

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Hawfi instead attaches “to warn” to qiyaman, an analysis the author rejects as grammatically unsound.
rows.anchor: وزعم الحوفي أنه متعلق بقيما وليس بقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God, the Book, or the Prophet may be understood as the subject of the warning and glad-tiding verbs.
rows.anchor: والفاعل ضمير الجلالة وكذا في الفعلين المعطوفين عليه وجوز أن يكون الفاعل في الكل ضمير الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning verb takes two objects; its first object, the unbelievers in the Book, is omitted as obvious, while “severe punishment” is retained as the point of emphasis.
rows.anchor: وحذف هنا المفعول الأول واقتصر على الثاني وهو قوله تعالى : ( بأسا شديدا ( إيذانا بأن ما سيق له الكلام هو المفعول الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The severe punishment primarily means the afterlife's punishment, though a broader view includes worldly punishment too.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد من البأس الشديد عذاب الآخرة لا غير وقيل يحتمل أن يندرج فيه عذاب الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min ladunhu means coming from God's presence as punishment for disbelief and is a second adjective of “punishment”; Qatada glosses ladun as ʿinda, while al-Raghib says it more narrowly marks an interval's endpoint, though others call it more emphatic and specific.
rows.anchor: من لدنه ( أي صادرا من عنده تعالى نازلا من قبله بمقابلة كفرهم

rows.speaker: أبو بكر عن عاصم
rows.claim: Abu Bakr's reading from Asim uses ishmaam on the dal, a kasra on the nun for two adjacent vowelless letters, and a kasra on the ha by assimilation; the majority read the dal and ha with damma, and Ibn Kathir links the ha with waw.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو بكر عن عاصم بإشمام الدال بمعنى تضعيف الصوت بالحركة الفاصلة بين الحرفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second account of ishmaam as a lip gesture on a vowelless dal is criticized as impossible medially; the objection and its answer are discussed, and the author says his preceding explanation removes the difficulty.
rows.anchor: في الدر المصون وغيره بأن هذا الإشمام إنما يتحقق في الوقف على الآخر وكونه في الوسط كما هنا لا يتصور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “and gives glad tidings” is accusative, coordinated with “to warn”; an anomalous reading has it in the nominative.
rows.anchor: والفاعل ضمير الجلالة وكذا في الفعلين

rows.speaker: صاحب حل العقد
rows.claim: One grammatical analysis treats fima as an appositive replacing the entire “He made no crookedness” clause; Abu Hayyan notes that clause-for-noun apposition is disputed.
rows.anchor: صاحب حل العقد : يمكن أن يكون فيما بدلا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another analysis makes the waw parenthetical and reverses the order, “a book upright, with no crookedness”; Ibn Abbas and Mujahid are reported to say this, and al-Samin explains that an intervening parenthesis is effectively removed from its position.
rows.anchor: مروي عن ابن عباس ومجاهد فإن الأول ترجمان القرآن

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisai read “gives glad tidings” in the light form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي ( ويبشر ) بالتخفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are those who affirm the Book, as the context suggests, and their mention follows the grace of revelation; righteous deeds are the works it teaches.
rows.anchor: المؤمنين ( أي المصدقين بالكتاب كما يشعر به وكذا بما تقدم ذكر ذلك بعد الإمتنان بإنزال الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present tense in “who do righteous deeds” signals renewed and continued action, and the relative clause follows “believers” because faith is the basis for work's acceptance.
rows.anchor: وإيثار صيغة الإستقبال في الصلة للإشعار بتجدد العمل واستمراره وإجراء الموصول على موصوفه المذكور

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and others identify the good reward as Paradise, with its lasting delights and immense recompense.
rows.anchor: هو كما قال السدي وغيره الجنة وفيها من النعيم المقيم والثواب العظيم ما فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers remain in their reward forever, with no end to their stay; “remaining” is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in “for them,” and both adverbs modify it.
rows.anchor: ماكثين فيه ( أي مقيمين في الأجر ( أبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning precedes glad tidings to emphasize deterring unbelievers and to put purification before adornment; warning is repeated in the next verse.
rows.anchor: وتقديم الإنذار على التبشير لإظهار كمال العناية بزجر الكفار عما هم عليه مع مراعاة تقديم التخلية على التحلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The renewed warning singles out a faction already included among those threatened, emphasizing the outrageousness of their disbelief: Arab polytheists said angels were daughters, Jews said Uzayr was God's son, and Christians said the Messiah was God's son.
rows.anchor: وهم العرب القائلون الملائكة بنات الله تعالى واليهود القائلون عزير ابن الله سبحانه والنصارى القائلون المسيح ابن الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaving “those who said” without the usual following description emphasizes that the statement itself suffices to mark the worst disbelief; the past tense confirms that they uttered it before.
rows.anchor: وترك إجراء الموصول على الموصوف كما في قوله تعالى : ( ويبشر المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some see an omission-and-recovery figure: the earlier warning omits its warned group and this warning omits the punishment; the author objects that this would exclude other unbelievers, though they could be included a fortiori because the son-claim is less than shirk.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية صنعة الاحتباك حيث حذف من الأول ما ذكر فيما بعد وهو المنذر وحذف مما بعد ما ذكر في الأول

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya's estimate of “the world” and Abu al-Baqa's estimate of “servants” make the warning encompass believers too; the author objects that this reduces warning to mere notice and leaves punishment unapplied to other groups of unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقدر ابن عطية العالم وأبو البقاء العباد فيعم المؤمنين أيضا وتعقب بأن التعميم يقتضي حمل الإنذار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claimants and their ancestors have no knowledge that God took a child—not merely because they failed to learn a knowable fact, but because such a thing is impossible; the negating min is emphatic.
rows.anchor: أي باتخاذه سبحانه وتعالى ولدا ( من علم ( مرفوع المحل على الإبتداء أو الفاعلية لاعتماد الظرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author favors taking “it” as the alleged child and the sentence as circumstantial; al-Mahdawi's analysis of the clause as an adjective of “child” is rejected.
rows.anchor: واستظهر كون ضمير ( به ) عايدا على الولد وعدم العلم وكذا حال الجملة على ما سمعت

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari takes “it” to refer to God: they know nothing of what is possible or impossible for Him.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري : هو عائد على الله تعالى على معنى ليس لهم علم بما يجوز عليه تعالى وما يمتنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their ancestors are also denied knowledge because they originated the attribution and serve as examples for their descendants.
rows.anchor: والتعرض لنفي العلم عنهم لأنهم قدوة هؤلاء

rows.speaker: الأخفش والمبرد
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad treat “great” as an exclamatory form: its implicit subject is the utterance, and “a word” is an accusative specification, meaning “how great a word.”
rows.anchor: ذهب الأخفش والمبرد إلى إلحاقه بباب التعجب فالفاعل هنا ضمير يرجع إلى قوله تعالى : ( اتخذ

rows.speaker: الفارسي وأكثر النحاة
rows.claim: Al-Farisi and most grammarians classify “great” with the praise/blame verbs niʿma and biʾsa and apply their syntactic rules; Abu Hayyan also allows an omitted object of blame described as a word coming from their mouths.
rows.anchor: وذهب الفارسي وأكثر النحاة إلى إلحاقه بباب نعم وبئس فيثبت له جميع أحكامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “coming from their mouths” describes the word and stresses their audacity: an evil idea may occur inwardly but normally is not spoken aloud.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى ( تخرج من أفواههم ( صفة ( كلمة ) تفيد استعظام اجترائهم على النطق بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the statement a “word” follows the usage of naming an entire poem by a single word.
rows.anchor: وتسميت ذلك كلمة على حد تسمية القصيدة بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reads kaburat with a vowelless ba, a Tamimi dialect; this verb also occurs with a damma, a still vowel, or transfer of its vowel to the first consonant.
rows.anchor: وقريء ( كبرت ) بسكون الباء وهي لغة تميم وجاء في نحو هذا الفعل ضم العين وتسكينها

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن يعمر وابن محيصن والقواس
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, Ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn Muhaysin, and al-Qawwas from Ibn Kathir read kalimatan in the nominative as the grammatical subject; the accusative reading is more emphatic.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وابن يعمر وابن محيصن والقواس عن ابن كثير ( كلمة ) بالرفع على الفاعلية والنصب أبلغ وأوكد

rows.speaker: النظام
rows.claim: Al-Nazzam uses the description “coming out of their mouths” to argue that speech is a body; the reply says air carrying speech physically exits while speech, as a quality, is figuratively said to exit.
rows.anchor: واستدل النظام على أن الكلام جسم بهذه الآية لوصفه فيها بالخروج الذي هو من خواص الأجسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nazzam instead regards speech as qualified air, not a quality; his argument assumes the literal sense is primary, but the author says the dispute is verbal and has no practical result.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأن النظام القائل بجسمية الكلام يقول هو الهواء المكيف لا الكيفية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their only statements on this matter are lies that cannot possibly be true; the closing pronouns refer to the claimants and their forefathers.
rows.anchor: إن يقولون إلا كذبا ﴾ أي ما يقولون في ذلك الشأن إلا قولا كذبا لا يكاد يدخل تحت إمكان الصدق

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي وابن جبير وابن عباس
rows.claim: Baakhiʿ means killing oneself; this sense is transmitted from Mujahid, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Abbas, while the authentic Bukhari wording glosses it as destroying oneself.
rows.anchor: وفي معناه ما في صحيح البخاري مهلك والأول مروي عن مجاهد والسدي وابن جبير وابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن الأزرق
rows.claim: Ibn al-Azraq cites Labid's verse using baakhiʿ for destroying oneself from longing; al-Layth glosses the verb as self-killing from intense grief, and the author also cites al-Farazdaq.
rows.anchor: وأنشد لابن الأزرق إذ سأله قول لبيد بن ربيعة : لعلك يوما إن فقدت مزارها على بعده يوما لنفسك باخع

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisai compares baakhʿ to weakening soil by repeated cultivation, and al-Zamakhshari explains it as reaching the bukhāʿ artery inside the nape; Ibn al-Athir and others say lexicons and anatomy do not attest that artery, though the author trusts al-Zamakhshari's expertise.
rows.anchor: وهو من بخع الأرض بالزراعة أي جعلها ضعيفة بسبب متابعة الزراعة كما قال الكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading joins baakhiʿ to nafsika by possessive construction, contrary to the expected active participle when it meets its conditions; al-Kisai says construct and governed forms are equivalent, while Abu Hayyan prefers the construction.
rows.anchor: وقريء ( باخع نفسك ) بالإضافة وهي خلاف الأصل في اسم الفاعل إذا استوفى شروط العمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “After them” means after their turning away and distancing themselves from faith, rather than after their deaths in disbelief.
rows.anchor: على آثارهم ( أي من بعدهم يعني من بعد توليهم عن الإيمان وتباعدهم عنه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that named Quraysh leaders gathered while the Prophet was deeply distressed by their rejection of his message; this occasion of revelation is more fitting than taking the phrase to mean after their deaths in disbelief.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن مردويه عن ابن عباس أن عتبة بن ربيعة وشيبة بن ربيعة وأبا جهل بن هشام والنضر بن الحرث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “This discourse” is the Qur'an, called the magnificent Book earlier; calling it hadith does not harm Ashʿari theologians who say its recited wording is originated.
rows.anchor: الجليل الشأن وهو القرآن المعبر عنه في صدر السورة بالكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional clause after in is the condition and its consequence is omitted because the preceding context makes it clear; another parsing treats “perhaps you will destroy yourself” as a fronted consequence postponed in meaning.
rows.anchor: وإن شرطية والجملة بعدها فعل الشرط والجواب محذوف ثقة بدلالة ما سبق عليه عند الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternate reading opens the hamza of an, supplying a causal li and attaching the clause to baakhiʿ; some deny an active participle can govern a past event, but the author replies that future grief can be caused by a past event and ongoing grief makes the case stronger.
rows.anchor: وقريء ( أن لم يؤمنوا ) بفتح همزة أن على التقدير الجار أي لأن وهو متعلق بباخع على أنه علة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One objection says that treating nonbelief as a past cause would make the destruction past if the cause is complete, or impossible if incomplete; the reply is that it is a motive, not a complete cause, so it need not precede the result in that way.
rows.anchor: وجه ذلك في الكشف بأنه إذا كانت البخع عدم الإيمان فإن كانت العلة قد تمت فالمعلول كذلك ضرورة تحقق المعلول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that a past-cause analysis weakens the Prophet's grief is rejected: present grief over past rejection, especially when it persists or recurs, can intensify the rhetoric; the verse may favor a continuing or future reading.
rows.anchor: وتعقب أيضا بأنه لا وجه له بل المبالغة في هذا أقوى لأنه إذا صدر منه لأمر مضى فكيف لو استمر أو تجدد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asafan can be an object of reason for baakhiʿ, a circumstantial accusative meaning sorrowful, or an absolute accusative with an omitted verb; al-Zajjaj says it is intense grief and anger.
rows.anchor: بباخع على أنه مفعول من أجله وجوز أن يكون حالا من الضمير فيه

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib says asaf can mean grief and anger together or separately: both begin as a stirring of the heart's blood toward vengeance, becoming outward anger against a weaker opponent and inward grief against a stronger one; Ibn Abbas says they share an origin but differ in expression.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب : الأسف الحزن والغضب معا وقد يقال لكل منهما على الانفراد وحقيقته ثوران دم القلب

rows.speaker: منذر بن سعد
rows.claim: Mundhir ibn Sad distinguishes grief for someone outside one's control from anger toward someone under one's control, explaining asaf here as grief but its use in 43:55 as anger.
rows.anchor: وإلى كون الأسف أعم من الحزن والغضب وكون الحزن على من لا يملك ولا هو تحت يد الآسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When paired with anger, asaf can denote grief separately, as in Moses' return to his people; Qatada gives anger in one report and grief in another, Bukhari gives regret, Mujahid gives anguish, and most interpreters say grief.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة تفسير الأسف هنا بالغضب وفي رواية أخرى بالحزن وفي صحيح البخاري تفسيره بالندم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laʿalla can express hope or apprehension; here it is an idiomatic expression of compassionate concern, consoling the Prophet and urging him to stop grieving over their unbelief.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أنها هنا للإشفاق الذي يقصد به التسلي والحث على ترك التحزن والتأسف

rows.speaker: العسكري
rows.claim: Al-Askari says laʿalla functions here as a prohibition, effectively “do not destroy yourself”; another view makes it interrogative, which Ibn Atiyya calls a denial, and the author suggests al-Askari may intend the consoling concern he prefers.
rows.anchor: وقال العسكري : هي هنا موضوعة موضع النهي كأنه قيل لا تبخع نفسك وقيل موضع الإستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many commentators see a representational metaphor: the Prophet's grief at his people's rejection is like one expected to kill himself after losing beloved companions through separation; this is preferable to analyzing isolated metaphorical words.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية عند غير واحد استعارة تمثيلية وذلك أنه مثل حاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A simile is also proposed because the Prophet and the self-killer are both explicit, but the author regards that comparison as remote.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن تكون من باب التشبيه لذكر طرفيه وهما النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent scope of “whatever is on earth” includes all nonrational things—animals, plants, and minerals—as adornment for the earth and its people, each according to its nature.
rows.anchor: الظاهر عموم ما جميع ما لا يعقل أي سواء كان حيوانا أو نباتا أو معدنا أي جعلنا جميع ما عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some exclude harmful animals and plants; advocates of the general reading answer that everything has some benefit, if only as evidence for the Maker and His oneness.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا يدخل في ذلك ما فيه إيذاء من حيوان ونبات ومن قال بعموم قال : لا شيء مما على الأرض إلا وفيه جهة انتفاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some restrict the adornment to particular examples: trees and rivers, flowering useful plants, animals of varied form and benefit, or precious metals and gems.
rows.anchor: وقص بعضهم ما بالأشجار والأنهار وآخر بالنبات لما فيه من الأزهار المختلفة الألوان والمنافع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One group restricts the adornment to greenery, water, livestock, clothes, and fruit; the author says this cannot stand as an exhaustive interpretation of a general expression.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة : أريد بها الخضرة والمياه والنعم والملابس والثمار ولعمري إنه تخصيص لا يقبله الخواص

rows.speaker: ابن جبير والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan are reported to interpret “whatever” as men; Ibn Abbas as scholars; and Ikrima as caliphs, scholars, and emirs. The author finds a strictly rational referent unlikely and suggests examples of humans may stand for the whole by predominance.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن ( ما ) هنا لمن يعقل والمراد بذلك على ما أخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن ابن جبير والحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “whatever” includes both rational and nonrational beings, with accountable people appearing as adornment in one respect and as subjects of trial in another; 18:46 likewise calls wealth and children adornment, contrary to al-Qadi's exclusion of the tested person from the adornment.
rows.anchor: وقد يقال : المراد بما عموم ما لا يعقل ومن يعقل فيدخل من توجه إليه التكليف وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If jaʿal means transformation, zīna is its second object; if it means creation, zīna is a purpose-object. The first lam modifies zīna or describes it, the second attaches to jaʿal, and the plural pronoun refers to earth's inhabitants or to the adorned things.
rows.anchor: ونصب ( زينة ) على أنه مفعول ثان للجعل إن حمل على معنى التصيير أو على أنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hisham ibn al-Hakam is said to permit attributing trial to God because he mistakenly thought God learns events only after they occur; Sunnis reject this and affirm God's eternal knowledge of particulars and universals.
rows.anchor: وجوز ذلك على الله سبحانه هشام بن الحكم بناء على جهله وزعمه أنه عز وجل لا يعلم الحوادث إلا بعد وجودها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trial means God treats people as if testing them so He can reward each fittingly; the best deed is asceticism toward worldly adornment, not being deceived by it, using it lawfully, fulfilling its rights, giving thanks, and reflecting on it as a path to knowing its Maker.
rows.anchor: وأول هذه الآية أن المراد ليعاملهم معاملة من يختبرهم ( أيهم أحسن عملا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Asked by Ibn Umar which people do best, the Prophet answered: those most intelligent, most abstinent from God's prohibitions, and quickest in obedience.
rows.anchor: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن الأحسن عملا كما أخرج ذلك ابن جرير وابن أبي حاتم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the best in deeds are those who abandon worldly life most, and a similar view is transmitted from Sufyan al-Thawri.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن الحسن أنه قال : أحسنهم عملا أشدهم للدنيا تركا وأخرج نحوه عن سفيان الثوري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other definitions rank the ascetic content with a traveler's provision highest, one who lawfully earns and spends well next, and one who gathers lawful and unlawful wealth for desires as blameworthy; the Prophet's answer is best.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعضهم أن الأحسن من زهد وقنع من الدنيا بزاد المسافر ووراءه وهو من استكثر من حلالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the trial includes both good and bad deeds, the comparative “best” is retained because the primary aim of worldly adornment is to reveal the excellence of those who excel.
rows.anchor: وإيراد صيغة التفضيل مع أن الابتلاء شامل للفريقين باعتبار أعمالهم المنقسمة إلى الحسن والقبيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayyuhum may be an interrogative subject with aḥsanu as predicate; the question clause is suspended from nبلو because that verb evokes inquiry or consideration.
rows.anchor: وأي إما إستفهامية فهي مرفوعة بالابتداء وأحسن خبرها والجملة في محل نصب بفعل الابتلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, ayyuhum is a relative pronoun meaning “the one who,” built on damma and appositional to the object pronoun in nبلوهم; al-Bahr says Sibawayh permits rather than requires this construction when the relative clause's head is omitted, a point the author finds difficult.
rows.anchor: وإما موصولة بمعنى فهي مبنية على الضم محلها النصب على أنها بدل من ضمير النصب في ( نبلوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥsanu remains a true comparative with its comparison omitted: God tests which people do better than those who are less good in deeds.
rows.anchor: والمفضل عليه محذوف والتقدير كما قال أبو حيان
